name: Spirit
title: Spirit: the geologist that outlived its plan
note: Illustrations are AI-generated artwork based on the verified events; every fact and its source come from the research dossiers. Narration is written for short, clear audio (~50 words).

closing.title: thank you, Spirit
closing.text: Planned for three months, it worked for more than six years and drove 7.7 km across Gusev Crater.

parts.title: Earth
parts.blurb: Before Mars: a dream, two failures, a decision, a name, a launch and a landing, told as a comic.

parts.title: Mars
parts.blurb: Six years in Gusev Crater: from a rebooting computer to a summit to a trap of sand.

beats.title: A geologist on wheels
beats.summary: Cornell geologist Steve Squyres dreams of a robotic field geologist. Over ten years he writes four proposals to NASA; the first three are rejected.
beats.narration: Nineteen eighty-seven. Geologist Steve Squyres, of Cornell University, dreams of a robotic field geologist: a rover carrying the tools a geologist would pack for the field. Over ten years he writes four proposals to NASA. The first three are rejected, but each one makes the idea better.

beats.title: Two losses in ten weeks
beats.summary: NASA loses the Mars Climate Orbiter and then the Mars Polar Lander. The agency has to rethink how it goes to Mars.
beats.narration: Autumn, 1999. NASA loses two missions to Mars in ten weeks. On September twenty-third, the Climate Orbiter burns up in the atmosphere: one team used imperial units, another metric, and it arrived about one hundred seventy kilometers too low. On December third, the Polar Lander is lost on arrival.

beats.title: Two rovers, not one
beats.summary: NASA announces two identical science rovers for 2003 instead of one. They will land far apart, doubling the science and adding a safety net.
beats.narration: August tenth, 2000. NASA announces it will send two big science rovers to Mars in 2003, not one. Ed Weiler, who leads space science, calls it incredibly exciting. Identical twins landing in very different places: twice the science, and a safety net if one of them fails.

beats.title: A girl names them
beats.summary: At Kennedy Space Center, nine-year-old Sofi Collis reveals the names of the twin rovers: Spirit and Opportunity.
beats.narration: June eighth, 2003. At Kennedy Space Center, nine-year-old Sofi Collis reveals the names of the twin rovers: Spirit and Opportunity. Born in Siberia and adopted at two, she won a contest of almost ten thousand essays. She wrote about looking at the stars from an orphanage, and dreaming of flying there.

beats.title: Liftoff
beats.summary: A Delta II lifts off from Cape Canaveral with Spirit aboard, a rover the size of a golf cart. Its twin follows 27 days later.
beats.narration: June tenth, 2003. A Delta Two rocket lifts off from Cape Canaveral carrying Spirit, a rover about the size of a golf cart. Four months earlier, the space shuttle Columbia was lost, and Spirit's landing site will carry its name. Its twin, Opportunity, will follow twenty-seven days later.

beats.title: Twenty-eight bounces
beats.summary: Spirit hits Gusev Crater inside a ball of airbags and bounces twenty-eight times before it stops, 13 km from its target.
beats.narration: January third, 2004, eight thirty-five pm, Pacific time. Spirit hits Mars inside a ball of airbags at about fourteen meters per second, and bounces twenty-eight times before rolling to a stop in Gusev Crater, a possible ancient lake. It lands thirteen kilometers from its target, but safe.

beats.title: Sol 18: a rover in a loop
beats.summary: With its arm out toward a rock, Spirit's computer reboots over and over. Too many files fill its flash memory, and the working memory cannot cope.
beats.narration: January twenty-first, 2004, sol eighteen. Spirit has its arm out toward a rock called Adirondack when its computer starts rebooting, more than one hundred twenty-five times. Too many files fill its flash memory, and the working memory cannot manage them. The longest test before launch lasted only ten days.

beats.title: Wiped clean, back to work
beats.summary: Engineers erase Spirit's flash memory and start over. The next day it brushes a rock, a first on another planet.
beats.narration: February fourth, 2004. Engineers erase Spirit's flash memory and rebuild its file system from scratch, like reformatting a broken computer. The next day, Spirit brushes a rock named Adirondack for five minutes, the first rock cleaned on another planet. The spot comes out much darker than the dust around it.

beats.title: Driving backwards
beats.summary: Spirit's front right wheel is failing, so it starts driving in reverse and drags it like an anchor, using it only on the hardest ground.
beats.narration: July fifteenth, 2004. Spirit has driven over three and a half kilometers, six times its design distance, but its front right wheel is failing: its motor draws three times the current of the others. The fix: drive backwards, dragging that wheel like an anchor and using it only when needed.

beats.title: A cleaning wind
beats.summary: Dust has choked Spirit's solar panels. Then a dust devil seems to sweep them clean, and its power jumps by about half.
beats.narration: March ninth, 2005, sol four hundred twenty. Spirit's solar panels are caked in dust, and its power has fallen to a few hundred watt-hours a day. Then, engineers think, a dust devil sweeps over it. Power jumps by half. The next sol, its cameras catch two dust devils on the plain.

beats.title: The top of Husband Hill
beats.summary: Spirit reaches the summit of Husband Hill, the first hill ever climbed by a rover on Mars, and takes a 360° view of the crater.
beats.narration: September, 2005. Spirit reaches the top of Husband Hill, one hundred six meters above its landing site: the first hill ever climbed by a rover on Mars. It was built for flat ground, but every climb brought new rocks. From the summit, it takes three hundred sixty degree panoramas.

beats.title: Comanche
beats.summary: On Husband Hill's slope, Spirit studies a rock outcrop. Four years later, cleaned-up data show it is rich in carbonate, a sign of mild water.
beats.narration: December, 2005. On Husband Hill's slope, Spirit visits an outcrop named Comanche, but its thermal spectrometer is coated in dust, and the data stay a puzzle for four years. In twenty-ten, scientists correct them: about a quarter of the rock is carbonate, which only forms in mild, neutral water.

beats.title: Sol 779: the wheel dies
beats.summary: The motor of Spirit's front right wheel fails for good and the wheel locks. Spirit will drag it from now on.
beats.narration: March thirteenth, 2006, sol seven hundred seventy-nine. Spirit's front right wheel motor dies for good, and the wheel locks. Spirit will have to drag it like a stuck shopping cart wheel. The next day it still drives ten meters, while engineers at JPL rehearse five-wheel moves with a replica rover in a sandbox.

beats.title: Silica from a broken wheel
beats.summary: Spirit's dragging wheel digs a trench that gleams white. It is almost pure silica, a record on Mars and a sign of hot water.
beats.narration: Two thousand seven. Spirit drags its dead wheel near Home Plate and digs a trench that gleams white. Its spectrometer says silica, and its X-ray instrument finds more than ninety percent, a record on Mars. On Earth, so much silica needs hot water reacting with rock: a warm, wet, possibly habitable past.

beats.title: Sinking at Troy
beats.summary: Driving backwards, Spirit breaks a dark crust and sinks into soft, bright sand hidden beneath it. The place is nicknamed Troy.
beats.narration: April, 2009. Driving backwards west of Home Plate, Spirit's wheels break through a dark crust and sink into bright, soft sand hidden underneath. The place is nicknamed Troy. The sand barely holds together, so the wheels find no grip. Spirit was planned for three months. It has worked for more than five years.

beats.title: Free Spirit
beats.summary: After months of rehearsals with test rovers on Earth, NASA starts the rescue: drive out along the rover's own tracks.
beats.narration: November sixteenth, 2009, sol two thousand eighty-seven. After months of rehearsals with test rovers on Earth, NASA sends the first commands of Free Spirit. The plan: drive forward, to the north, exactly along its own tracks, dragging its dead wheel. A pointed rock under the rover's belly makes every meter delicate.
facts: Drive out on its own tracks

beats.title: A rover becomes a station
beats.summary: After months of failed attempts, NASA declares Spirit a stationary research platform. Its new goals: survive the winter and study Mars' wobble.
beats.narration: January twenty-sixth, 2010. After months of failed attempts, NASA declares Spirit a stationary research platform. Doug McCuistion says: Spirit is not dead; it has just entered another phase of its long life. The new goals: survive the Martian winter, and measure the planet's tiny wobble to learn about its core.

beats.title: The last message
beats.summary: Winter closes in: Spirit's panels face away from the Sun and its electronics fall to −41.5 °C. That day, it sends its last signal.
beats.narration: March twenty-second, 2010. Winter is closing in. Spirit's solar panels face away from the Sun, and its electronics have dropped to minus forty-one point five degrees Celsius. Power falls to one hundred thirty-three watt-hours, below the threshold the team feared. That day, Spirit sends its last signal to Earth.

beats.title: The silence is declared
beats.summary: After more than 1,300 commands with no answer, NASA ends its attempts to reach Spirit. Built for three months, it worked for over six years.
beats.narration: May twenty-fourth, 2011. After more than one thousand three hundred commands with no answer, NASA ends its attempts to contact Spirit. Built for three months, it worked for over six years and drove seven point seven kilometers. Engineers think its insides fell to about minus fifty-five Celsius, too cold to wake.

beats.title: New lessons in old data
beats.summary: Researcher Paulo de Souza merges 32 old soil measurements from Spirit and finds crystalline hematite and magnetite in ordinary Martian soil.
beats.narration: Twenty twenty-six. Researcher Paulo de Souza revisits Spirit's old data. He merges thirty-two soil measurements from its iron spectrometer into one signal, like six days of continuous work. It shows crystalline hematite and magnetite in ordinary Martian soil: a hint, not proof, that water was once widespread.
